title: "Cubic Spline Interpolation"
output: html_document
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

## Overview

This example demonstrates cubic spline interpolation using the `aoclda` package. A
cubic spline constructs a smooth, twice continuously differentiable curve that passes
through a set of data points.

```{r library}
library(aoclda)
```

## Data

We sample `sin(x)` at 10 uniformly spaced interpolation sites in the interval `[0, 9]`.

```{r data}
n_sites <- 10
x <- seq(0, 9, length.out = n_sites)
y <- sin(x)
```

## Fit a natural cubic spline

```{r fit}
spline <- cubic_spline$new(spline_type = "natural")
spline$fit(x, y)
```

## Evaluate the spline

The spline can be evaluated at any set of query points. Points at the interpolation
sites reproduce the original data values.

```{r evaluate}
x_eval <- seq(0, 9, length.out = 50)
values <- spline$evaluate(x_eval)
head(values)

# At the interpolation sites the spline reproduces the original data values.
all.equal(spline$evaluate(x), y)
```

## Evaluate derivatives

Passing a vector of `orders` evaluates several derivatives at once. Here we request the
value (order 0) and the first derivative (order 1); the result is a matrix whose rows
correspond to the requested orders.

```{r derivatives}
deriv <- spline$evaluate(x_eval, orders = c(0, 1))
deriv
```

## Piecewise polynomial coefficients

The fitted spline can be inspected through its per-cell cubic coefficients, stored in
ascending power order `[c0, c1, c2, c3]` along the columns (one row per cell).

```{r coefficients}
print(spline$coefficients)
```

## Locate query points

`search_cells` returns, for each query point, the 0-based index of the cell that
contains it.

```{r search}
cells <- spline$search_cells(c(0.5, 4.5, 8.5))
print(cells)
```
